name: Kano Model
use_case: A survey-based classification of product attributes by how their presence or absence affects customer satisfaction, sorting them into must-be features whose absence causes anger, one-dimensional features where more is better, and delighters that please precisely because nobody expected them. Best used when deciding how much to invest in polish versus novelty, and when a team cannot tell which items are table stakes that earn no credit and which will actually differentiate.
strengths: distinguishes features that earn credit from those that merely avoid anger
the paired functional and dysfunctional questions resist wishful answers
explains why heavy investment in must-be attributes moves no metric
tracks how delighters decay into expectations over time
weaknesses: requires a real survey with real customers, not a workshop guess
the questionnaire is easy to word badly and hard to interpret
classifies attributes but says nothing about cost or effort
categories drift as the market matures, so results need refreshing
use_cases: Residents keep complaining about the city's online services portal, and the digital team wants to learn which service features people simply expect to work and which extras would genuinely raise their satisfaction.

A nursing school is redesigning its clinical placements and wants the students to tell it which parts of the training they take for granted and which additions would make the experience noticeably better.
We spent a year making the product faster and more reliable, yet customer satisfaction scores did not move, and we want to understand why that investment earned no credit with users.

A hotel chain wants to know whether guests are still pleased by free Wi-Fi and early check-in, or whether those amenities have become basic expectations that only draw complaints when they are missing.
